WHO WE ARE
IEX is India’s premier electricity exchange providing a nationwide, automated trading platform 
for physical delivery of electricity, renewable energy and certificates including renewable energy 
certificates as well as energy saving certificates. The exchange platform enables efficient price 
discovery and increases accessibility and transparency of the energy market in India, while 
also enhancing the speed and efficiency of trade execution. The Exchange is ISO Certified for 
Quality Management, Information Security Management and Environment Management since 
August 2016. Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) is a publicly listed company with NSE and BSE since 
October 2017 and is approved and regulated by Central Electricity Regulatory Commission since  
27 June 2008.

IEX ACADEMY
IEX Academy, an initiative of Indian Energy Exchange which aims to enhance expertise across the power sector. Launched in June 2023, it 
serves as a learning platform, bringing together industry professionals with interest in power markets. Through self-paced learning courses, 
specialized certification programs, and residential training workshops for corporates with subject-matter experts and permiere institutions, 
IEX Academy equips participants with valuable skills and insights to navigate a rapidly evolving energy landscape.

A RESILIENT AND FUTURE-READY POWER SECTOR
Electricity is one of the key enablers of India’s economic transformation. As the nation 
advances towards becoming a global manufacturing and digital powerhouse, the power 
sector continues to evolve with greater scale, reliability and technological integration. 
Over the past decade, the country’s power sector 
ecosystem has undergone remarkable transition - from 
addressing shortages and expanding access to building 
a modern, resilient and future-ready energy infrastructure 
- capable of supporting sustained economic growth. 
India’s power demand trajectory reflects the pace 
of the country’s development. Rapid urbanisation, 
rising industrial activity, infrastructure expansion and 
increasing digital adoption are continuously driving 
electricity consumption upward. During FY’26, India 
successfully met a peak power demand of 245 GW while 
reducing power shortages to just 0.03%, which marks 
a substantial improvement from 4.2% in FY’14. This 
transformation highlights the strengthening generation 
capacity, transmission networks and grid management 
systems across the country.
One of the most significant achievements of the sector 
has been the expansion of electricity access across 
India.  The world’s largest synchronous national grid now exceeds 5 lakh circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission 
lines. Through large-scale rural electrification and last-
mile connectivity initiatives, electricity today reaches 
nearly every village and household in the country. Flagship 
programmes such as Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti 
Yojana  (DDUGJY), Integrated Power Development Scheme 
(IPDS) and Saubhagya accelerated the creation of modern 
distribution infrastructure and enabled electricity access 
for nearly 30 million households. Improved supply 
reliability has positively impacted education, healthcare, 
agriculture and small enterprises, particularly in rural and 
semi-urban India.
The sector’s evolution is also visible in the steady 
improvement in quality and availability of power supply. 
Average daily power supply in rural India has increased 
substantially over the last decade, while urban areas 
continue to witness near-round-the-clock availability. 
Per capita electricity consumption in India has also 
risen to 1,460 kilowatt-hours in FY’25, registering an 
6 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statements
=== page 11 ===
• 
/ 
increase of about 53% compared with 957 kilowatt-
hours a decade ago. This is reflective of improved living 
standards, growing appliance ownership and holistic 
economic participation.
Alongside infrastructure growth, India’s power 
ecosystem is becoming increasingly technology-
driven. The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme 
(RDSS) is accelerating deployment of smart meters, 
digital monitoring systems and modernised distribution 
infrastructure to improve operational efficiency and 
consumer experience. With over 5.6 crore smart meters 
installed across the country, consumers are gaining 
better visibility and control over electricity consumption 
while utilities benefit from improved billing efficiency and 
network management.
India’s renewable energy transition has further 
strengthened the sector’s long-term sustainability. The 
country today ranks among global leaders in renewable 
energy capacity, with solar and wind energy capacity 
witnessing unprecedented growth. India achieved a 
significant milestone in July 2025 when non-fossil fuel 
sources constituted over 50% of the country’s installed 
electricity capacity. This marked a major step in India’s 
clean energy transition, reflecting the growing maturity of 
the country’s renewable energy ecosystem and its ability 
to integrate clean energy into the national grid.
Continued investments in transmission infrastructure 
are ensuring that growing renewable capacity can be 
efficiently integrated and delivered across regions. The 
National Electricity Plan 2023–2032 outlines a strong roadmap for future-ready transmission systems, inter-
regional connectivity and grid expansion to support rising 
electricity demand and emerging energy applications.
The financial and operational performance of distribution 
utilities has also shown notable improvement. AT&C 
losses declined to 15% in FY’25 from 16% in FY’24, while 
the narrowing of the ACS-ARR gap and improved payment 
discipline across the value chain reflect the impact 
of sustained reforms and operational strengthening. 
Timely payments to generators and a growing focus on 
power procurement optimisation further underscore the 
sector’s transition towards greater financial discipline 
and operational efficiency. These developments are 
creating a healthier and more sustainable ecosystem for 
long-term sectoral growth.
As India’s economy continues to expand, electricity 
will remain central to industrial competitiveness, digital 
growth, urban development and sustainability ambitions. 
Emerging sectors such as electric mobility, data centres, 
green hydrogen and advanced manufacturing are 
expected to further accelerate demand for reliable and 
clean power.
In this evolving landscape, the Indian Energy Exchange 
(IEX) endeavors to remain at the forefront of technology-
enabled and market-driven solutions in ensuring 
efficiency, flexibility and transparency across the 
power ecosystem. India’s power sector today is not 
only supporting economic growth but also building 
the foundation for a more connected, sustainable and 
energy-secure future.

THE SHIFT TO SMARTER POWER PROCUREMENT
State power utilities in the country are steadily transforming how they procure electricity 
and the shift is already evident in the numbers. Across India, distribution companies 
are moving beyond traditional methods and involving power exchanges into their core 
supply planning processes. What was once an option to address short-term deficits 
or unexpected demand has evolved into a strategic procurement channel, guided by 
data-driven decision-making. On the strength of leveraging price signals, generation 
economics, and time-of-day demand patterns, utilities are adopting a more dynamic 
and informed approach to sourcing power.
This transformation is reshaping three critical elements 
of DISCOM operations: the timing of procurement 
decisions, the scheduling of State-allocated generation, 
and the daily optimisation of supply-demand balance. 
States such as Uttarakhand, West Bengal, and Punjab 
exemplify this shift, having embedded market-based 
procurement as a central pillar of their operational 
strategy.In Punjab, for instance, long-term PPAs had kept the 
load curve largely flat, but the State discom has shifted 
significant demand to daytime hours to tap surplus, low-
cost solar power. By actively tracking price trends and 
increasing participation in DAM, RTM, and the Green 
Day-Ahead Market on IEX, the State discom optimized 
costs, improved reliability, and supported sustainability 
goals, all reflected in a 50% CAGR in exchange purchases 
8 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statements
=== page 13 ===
• 
/ 
over five years. Once a seasonal buyer during the paddy 
season, Punjab now engages year-round by monitoring 
market signals and weather patterns. In FY’26, heavy 
rainfall reduced paddy-season demand across the 
State, enabling the State discom to sell surplus power 
on exchanges to the quantum of over 1 BU — unlocking 
new revenue while maintaining grid security and 
avoiding DSM penalties. This strategy of buying smartly 
and selling surplus positioned the State as a leader in 
market-based procurement and it also became the first 
government entity to acquire a private thermal plant, 
enhancing supply and liquidity.
Similarly, in West Bengal, which operates under different 
demand conditions, the State discom leveraged 
competitive exchange prices through a data-driven 
strategy. In FY’26, it procured nearly 7 BU from power 
exchanges, an increase of about 250% YoY, even as 
peak demand rose just 2%. By optimizing purchases at 
an average cost of nearly `3/unit, the State achieved 
significant savings. The discom’s strategy was to 
maximise low-cost solar hours on DAM and RTM, 
where average prices touched `2.34/unit and `2.51/
unit, respectively. Instead of running higher-cost thermal 
plants at full load, West Bengal operated them at technical 
minimum and met additional demand via cheaper 
exchange power. This reduced fuel use, cut costs, and 
enabled greater integration of renewable energy.
Uttarakhand has also integrated power exchanges into 
routine supply planning, using data-driven procurement 
and saved over `160 crore in FY’26, while also earning 
`125 crore from REC sales. Initially procuring via the 
DEEP (Discovery of Efficient Electricity Price) portal, the State discom shifted to a diversified strategy leveraging 
exchange products to lower costs. It sourced nearly 
850 MUs through long-duration contracts at about 
`3.59/unit and saved `160 crore overall. As a hydro-rich 
State, Uttarakhand generates surplus renewable energy 
beyond its RPO needs which it monetized by selling 35 
lakh RECs on exchanges at an average price of `350 per 
REC, generating `125 crore in additional revenue.
Power procurement trends from Telangana discoms 
also reveal market-based dynamic sourcing as a core 
operational strategy. Improved supply from renewables 
(solar, hydro, wind) alongside steady coal generation 
softened prices enabling discoms to replace costlier 
power with exchange-based procurement. Telangana 
capitalized on this opportunity through a data-driven 
approach. In FY’26, the State discoms procured about 13 
BU from exchanges at an average of `3.04/unit, saving 
around `700 crore.
The growing reliance on exchanges across States 
signals a lasting change in procurement strategy. Data 
from multiple regions shows measurable gains: lower 
purchase costs, better demand–supply balance and 
new revenue streams from surplus power. As renewable 
capacity continues to expand and hourly price variation 
becomes sharper, States that actively respond to market 
signals are likely to widen their financial advantage. 
Exchange-led procurement is therefore not just a short-
term tactic, it is becoming a defining feature of how 
India’s power system is planned and managed.

GREEN MARKETS: TECHNOLOGY ENABLING A 
SUSTAINABLE ENERGY FUTURE
India’s energy transition is no longer a vision for the future, it is a transition unfolding at a 
rapid pace. With non-fossil sources accounting for half of the country’s installed power 
capacity, the nation has entered a defining decade in its journey towards achieving its 
2030 climate commitments and 2070 commitment of net-zero emissions. Renewable 
energy has moved beyond incremental growth to become a fundamental pillar of India’s 
power system, delivering lower energy costs, reducing dependence on imported fuels, 
and reshaping electricity markets. 
As this transition gathers momentum, the challenge is 
no longer limited to adding renewable capacity. The next 
phase lies in integrating renewable energy efficiently 
into the grid. The growing share of solar and wind 
generation has introduced a new level of complexity to 
system operations. Their inherent variability has led to 
larger intra-day forecast deviations, sharper net-load 
ramps and more frequent real-time imbalances, making 
flexibility and responsive market mechanisms essential 
for maintaining grid reliability.
At IEX, we believe that well-designed markets are central 
to enabling this transformation. Over the years, we 
have continuously expanded our market architecture 
to address the evolving needs of India’s power sector, 
creating innovative products that enhance flexibility, improve price discovery and accelerate renewable 
energy adoption.
A significant milestone in this journey has been the 
creation of India’s first Green Market through the Green 
Day-Ahead Market (G-DAM) and the Green Term-Ahead 
Market (G-TAM). IEX has built transparent, market-
based avenues for energy procurement and trading. 
These products empower renewable-rich States to 
monetise surplus green power beyond their compliance 
obligations while enabling generators to adopt flexible 
procurement strategies, ranging from hybrid market-
PPA structures to fully market-based models. In doing 
so, IEX is strengthening the economic case for renewable 
energy while supporting the sustainability ambitions of 
both corporates and the nation at large.
12 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statements
=== page 17 ===
• 
/ 
The market response has been equally encouraging. As 
renewable generation has increased, green power prices 
have become increasingly competitive, encouraging 
greater participation in the Green Market. This has 
translated into strong growth in traded volumes across 
the Green Market, registering 23% YoY growth, with the 
Green Market accounting for nearly 8% of the electricity 
volume traded on the Exchange in FY’26. The increasing 
contribution of green market products to IEX’s overall 
product mix reflects the growing confidence of market 
participants in transparent, exchange-based renewable 
power procurement.
Alongside the Green Market, the Real-Time Market (RTM) 
has emerged as an indispensable pillar of renewable 
integration. As renewable penetration increases, balancing 
demand and supply closer to delivery has become critical. 
RTM enables market participants to respond to real-time 
system conditions through transparent price signals, 
improving economic dispatch, correcting imbalances 
efficiently and facilitating secure integration of renewable 
energy. For DISCOMs, particularly in renewable-rich states 
such as Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Andhra 
Pradesh, RTM has become a valuable tool for portfolio 
optimisation and reducing renewable energy curtailment 
by providing an efficient platform to sell surplus power. 
Reflecting its growing relevance and operational value, 
the RTM segment has recorded a five-year CAGR of 42% 
and in FY’26 accounted for 34% of the total electricity 
traded volume on IEX.
Beyond electricity trading, IEX is also enabling India’s 
sustainability ambitions through RECs and International 
Renewable Certificates (I-REC). The REC market, which 
commenced trading on power exchanges in 2011, has also played a pivotal role in enabling obligated entities 
to meet their Renewable Consumption Obligation 
(RCO) requirements while facilitating India’s broader 
decarbonisation journey. Going beyond national 
boundaries, through ICX, India’s first I-REC(E) issuer 
approved by the I-TRACK Foundation, ICX aims to make 
a global impact on the voluntary carbon market.
The evolution of India’s energy markets is also creating 
new opportunities beyond electricity trading. Battery 
Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are beginning to reshape 
system flexibility, with large-scale additions and declining 
discovered tariffs enabling merchant-based BESS 
transactions on the IEX. At the same time, the emerging 
regulatory framework for Carbon Credit Certificates is 
laying the foundation for transparent, market-based 
carbon trading, extending the principles of efficient price 
discovery from electricity to emissions management.
As clean energy adoption accelerates across industries, 
market-based mechanisms will play an increasingly 
strategic role in enabling India’s path to a low-carbon 
economy. Guided by innovation, transparency and 
efficiency, IEX remains committed to building markets 
that not only facilitate energy transition but also create 
enduring value for every stakeholder.
This commitment extends beyond markets. As India’s 
first carbon-neutral power exchange for three years 
running, IEX continues to demonstrate that sustainability 
and business growth can progress together, supporting 
the nation’s transition towards a cleaner, more resilient 
and future-ready energy ecosystem.

FROM EXCHANGE TO ENERGY MARKET ECOSYSTEM
The evolution of a successful institution is defined not only 
by its ability to grow, but also by its ability to identify new 
opportunities and build on its core strengths. Over the past 
eighteen years, IEX has consistently followed this path, evolving 
from India’s first power exchange into a diversified energy 
market ecosystem with a growing presence across multiple 
segments of the energy value chain.
Established in 2008, IEX has built its leadership on the  
foundation of technology, innovation and customer centricity. 
Through continuous investment in digital platforms, market 
innovation and customer focused solutions, the Exchange 
has consistently enhanced the trading experience for market 
participants while strengthening its position as India’s leading 
electricity marketplace. This commitment to innovation and 
operational excellence has enabled IEX to remain agile in 
a rapidly evolving energy landscape. As the organisation 
matured, so did its vision. The expertise gained from developing 
and scaling India’s largest electricity exchange, encompassing 
technology, market innovation, customer centric solutions and 
market design, created opportunities to extend IEX’s capabilities 
into adjacent energy markets. Leveraging these strengths, IEX 
embarked on a strategic journey of diversification, expanding 
into adjacent energy markets where its expertise could create 
long term value. EXPANDING BEYOND ELECTRICITY
India’s growing economy requires well-functioning markets 
across every major energy commodity. Electricity, natural gas, 
carbon and coal each have a distinct role to play in strengthening 
energy security, supporting industrial growth and enabling the 
country’s transition to a lower-carbon future.
With this long-term vision, IEX expanded beyond electricity by 
creating specialised exchanges designed to meet the unique 
requirements of each market while remaining anchored in 
the same core principles of transparency, efficiency and 
technology-driven price discovery.
The launch of Indian Gas Exchange (IGX) in 2020 marked the 
Company’s first step towards building a diversified energy 
market ecosystem extending IEX’s expertise to the natural 
gas sector and broadening its role in India’s evolving energy 
markets. This was followed by the establishment of ICX 
Private Limited (formerly known as International Carbon 
Exchange Private Limited), which serves as an authorised 
issuer of International Renewable Energy Certificates (I-RECs), 
supporting organisations in meeting their renewable energy 
and sustainability objectives. Looking ahead, the incorporation 
of Coal Exchange represents the next phase of this journey, 
bringing market-based solutions to another critical pillar of 
India’s energy economy. 
Together, these initiatives reflect IEX’s commitment to building 
the market infrastructure needed to support India’s evolving 
energy landscape.

Annual Report 2025-26 | 23
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsIGX – INDIA’S FIRST AND ONL Y 
AUTHORIZED NATIONAL LEVEL PHYSICAL 
DELIVERY-BASED GAS TRADING EXCHANGE
FY’26 marked an important milestone for the Indian Gas 
Exchange (“IGX”) as IGX’s electronic exchange platform 
(“Exchange”) completed five years of operations. Since its 
launch in 2020, IGX has facilitated in bringing transparency, 
efficiency and market-based price discovery to India’s natural 
gas sector. IGX has over last five years, established itself as an 
organized, transparent and technology-enabled marketplace 
for physical delivery of natural gas, facilitating participation 
from stakeholders including the gas producers, gas marketing 
companies, city gas distribution companies, power generation 
companies, refineries, fertilizer companies, terminal operators 
and industrial consumers. 
Natural gas and LNG have progressively solidified their position 
as critical pillars and have become the fundamental elements 
of the global energy landscape, functioning both as a versatile 
fossil fuel and as a strategic bridge in the transition toward 
lower-carbon energy systems 
The city gas distribution sector is expected to remain a key driver 
of natural gas demand growth in India, supported by ongoing 
expansion of infrastructure, increasing urbanization and fuel-
switching initiatives. IGX provides a transparent and organized 
platform that enables efficient trading of gas and supports the 
development of a market-driven gas ecosystem.
GROWING SCALE AND MARKET RELEVANCE
Since IGX commenced operations, the Exchange has witnessed 
significant growth in trading activity, with cumulative traded 
volumes of 76.79, 60.02 and 40.84 million Metric Million 
British Thermal Units (“million MMBtu”) in Fiscals 2026, 2025 
and 2024, respectively, growing at a CAGR of 37.12% between 
Fiscals 2024 and 2026. Monthly contracts are the undisputed 
backbone of IGX volumes, accounting for approximately 64% of the total Fiscal 2026 volumes. While monthly contracts lead, 
fortnightly and weekly contracts show significant traction.
Gas Index of India (“GIXI”), the Exchange’s flagship price index, 
continues to serve as a transparent, nationwide benchmark 
reflecting spot gas prices across delivery points, regions and 
the market as a whole for market participants. 
With this performance, IGX facilitated close to 2.82% of India’s 
total gas consumption in FY’26. As of FY’26, the Exchange’s 
platform comprised trading across 19 delivery points spanning 
five regional hubs and 10 contract types across the spot and 
forward markets.
During FY’26, IGX recorded a profit after tax of `418.68 million, 
registering a growth in profit after tax of 35.29% over the 
previous year. 
NEW CONTRACTS
During the year, the Exchange launched the Balance of Month 
(BoM) Contract, enabling market participants to procure or sell 
gas for the remaining days of an ongoing calendar month. This 
new offering complements IGX’s existing portfolio of spot and 
forward contracts and provides additional flexibility for short-
term gas procurement and risk management.
NEW DELIVERY POINTS
To further enhance physical market accessibility, IGX expanded 
its delivery options with the addition of the Palanpur delivery 
point during FY’26 strengthening connectivity between the 
Gujarat gas grid and demand centres in the Western and 
Northern regions. As of FY’26, IGX’s delivery framework 
comprised 19 delivery points across [five regional hubs - 
Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western and Central, spanning 
LNG terminals, pipeline intersection points and domestic gas 
fields. The continued expansion and diversification of delivery 
infrastructure strengthen market connectivity and provides 
participants with flexibility in procuring natural gas across 
regions.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsDIGITAL AND CAPABILITY BUILDING 
INITIATIVES
As part of its efforts to improve stakeholder engagement and 
market participation, IGX launched the IGX mobile application. 
The application enables market participants to access 
market information, track trades, prices and stay updated on 
developments in the gas market through a convenient digital 
platform.
IGX also launched its first IGX Certification Course (ICC) under 
the IGX Academy initiative. The programme has been designed 
on creating an understanding of the gas industry, including an 
overview of the Indian gas market, gas exchange regulations, 
market structure and product offerings, trading, clearing and 
settlement mechanisms, and familiarization with the trader 
workstation.
STRATEGIC COLLABORATIONS
IGX continued to strengthen its engagement with domestic 
and international stakeholders through strategic collaborations 
aimed at supporting the development of India’s gas market.
In September 2025, IGX signed a memorandum of 
understanding with PRISMA, European Capacity Platform 
GmbH, an international IT company that runs the PRISMA 
platform, Europe’s gas  capacity market platform, for 
cooperation and development of modern, transparent and 
efficient gas markets, explore digital solutions for trading gas 
and LNG along with exchanging knowledge and best practices.
In January 2026 IGX also signed a memorandum of 
understanding with Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited 
(HPCL) to develop regasification booking platform to enable 
market-driven booking of storage and regasification services 
at HPCL’s Chhara LNG Terminal.
RECOGNITION AND AWARDS
The achievements of IGX and its contribution towards the 
development of India’s natural gas market received industry 
recognition during FY’26.
IGX was selected as a finalist under at the Platts Global Energy 
Awards 2025 in the “Excellence in Energy – Downstream” 
category for the Exchange, and IGX’s Managing Director 
and Chief Executive Officer Mr. Rajesh Kumar Mediratta was 
shortlisted in the category “Chief Trailblazer of the Year”.
Further, IGX was recognised at the Future Energy Leaders 
Award Show (FELAS) 2026 and was declared the winner under 
the “Technovators-Natural Gas” category.ENABLING INDIA’S GAS-BASED ECONOMY
India’s natural gas market is expected to benefit from ongoing 
regulatory and policy initiatives aimed at enhancing market 
efficiency, improving infrastructure utilization and facilitating 
exchange-based gas trading. The PNGRB’s unified tariff 
framework (UFT), effective January 1, 2026, replaced the 
earlier 3-zone with a simplified 2-zone regime, reducing the 
cost of transporting gas across the national grid and improving 
pan-India arbitrage opportunities. The Oilfields (Regulation 
and Development) Amendment Act, 2025, which came into 
force on April 15, 2025, modernized the regulatory framework 
governing upstream oil and gas operations with the objective 
of accelerating domestic exploration and production. The 
PNGRB also proposed further reforms under the Petroleum 
and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (Access Code for Common 
Carrier or Contract Carrier Natural Gas Pipelines) Regulations, 
including a more transparent, flexible and consumer friendly 
capacity booking framework, including online, 24x7 capacity 
booking and booking on intraday and day-ahead basis and 
the establishment of an Independent System Operator (ISO). 
Collectively, these reforms are expected to enhance liquidity, 
improve price discovery and support the development of a 
more competitive and vibrant gas trading ecosystem in India.
These developments, together with continued expansion of the 
national gas pipeline grid and city gas distribution network, and 
the GOI’s stated objective of raising the share of natural gas in 
India’s primary energy mix from approximately 7% to 15% by 
2030, are expected to support the broader transition toward 
cleaner, more efficient and more flexible energy systems. During 
the year, the natural gas market was also affected by geopolitical 
uncertainty, particularly disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, 
which tightened global supply and drove sharp price volatility. 
As imported regasified LNG (RLNG) constituted a substantial 
share of gas traded on the Exchange, these disruptions 
together with elevated prices and the policy response under 
the Natural Gas (Supply Regulation) Order, 2026 contributed to 
a decline in RLNG trading volumes towards the end of FY’26, 
which subsequently recovered. Such geopolitical developments 
influence LNG availability, trading volumes and price discovery 
underscoring the importance of supply diversification and 
continued development of domestic gas sources for the long-
term resilience of India’s gas market.
Having completed five years of operations, IGX enters its 
next phase to expand trading volumes and liquidity across 
its exchange platform, capitalize on expected growth in the 
organized market for natural gas, expand its product offering, 
develop new gas market platforms and adjacent trading 
segments, continue its regulatory and policy advocacy to 
deepen the natural gas market in India, leverage its partnerships 
to develop derivatives and financial market integration and to 
invest in and expand IGX Academy to create awareness on gas 
exchange fundamentals.

Annual Report 2025-26 | 25
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsICX: BUILDING THE FOUNDATION FOR 
INDIA’S CLEAN ENERGY MARKETS
As India’s clean energy transition gathers pace, businesses are 
increasingly looking for credible and globally accepted ways 
to demonstrate their use of renewable electricity and advance 
their sustainability commitments. This growing need has 
accelerated the adoption of market-based instruments that 
bring transparency, credibility and international recognition to 
renewable energy consumption.
Recognising this opportunity, ICX the wholly owned subsidiary 
of IEX, took a pioneering step by bringing the globally recognized 
International Renewable Energy Certificates (I-REC(E)) 
framework to India. Accredited by the I-Track Foundation as the 
Local Issuer on 2nd September 2024, ICX has since emerged as 
a crucial enabler for corporates seeking to credibly demonstrate 
their renewable energy usage in line with international standards.
WHAT IS I-REC(E)?
The International Renewable Energy Certificate for Electricity 
[I-REC(E)] is a tradable Energy Attribute Certificate (EAC) 
that conveys verified information about the production 
of one megawatt-hour (1 MWh) of electricity such as its 
source, production facility, and its capacity. Accredited by the 
International Tracking Standard Foundation, I-REC(E) enables 
electricity users worldwide to credibly report renewable 
consumption for Scope 2 emissions, sustainability disclosures, 
and voluntary initiatives. By procuring I-REC(E), companies 
can claim renewable energy usage, reduce Scope 2 emissions, 
and align with leading global frameworks such as RE100 and 
the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi)—demonstrating 
measurable progress toward net-zero and sustainability goals.STRENGTHENING TRUST AND INTEGRITY
Building on IEX’s deep expertise in the Indian power sector, ICX 
has brought strong governance and credibility to the voluntary 
I-REC(E) market by tailoring international frameworks to India’s 
regulatory environment. Aligned with the I-TRACK standards 
and the I-REC(E) Code, ICX has instituted rigorous processes 
to ensure integrity, transparency, and the elimination of double 
counting. This includes conducting detailed analyses of Central 
and State regulations, embedding regulatory checks into device 
registration and certificate issuance, and proactively addressing 
challenges related to Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs). 
Additionally, ICX has streamlined the identification and 
treatment of banking quantum as per State-specific rules, 
ensuring robust compliance. Through these measures, ICX has 
added substantial value as the local I-REC(E) Issuer, fostering 
trust and confidence for corporates and stakeholders in India’s 
renewable energy certificate ecosystem. This has resulted in 
major shifts in the device (power plant) registration and I-REC(E) 
issuance processes leading to increased confidence among 
market participants and the product’s market value. The impact 
of this initiative is already being felt on the ground. By enabling 
access to I-REC(E), ICX has provided Indian corporates with 
the same credibility and recognition enjoyed by their peers 
globally. This international parity has not only strengthened 
ESG disclosures but also enhanced investor confidence in the 
country’s corporate sustainability journey.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsDEVELOPING A ROBUST MARKET

ICX has worked extensively with renewable energy generators, 
corporates and ecosystem participants to build awareness,

I-REC(E) across the country. These efforts have translated into 
strong market growth. During FY’26, the India I-REC(E) market 
recorded a 53% year-on-year increase in certificate issuances, 
rising from 12.01 million certificates in FY’25 to 18.41 million 
certificates in FY’26. The market also witnessed a 49% growth 
in new renewable energy facility registrations, increasing from 
411 facilities in FY’25 to 614 facilities in FY’26. The continued

energy generators and rising demand from corporates seeking 
credible solutions for Scope 2 emissions reduction and globally 
recognised sustainability reporting.
EXPANDING IEX’S DIVERSIFICATION 
JOURNEY
The development of India’s I-REC(E) market represents an 
important milestone in the diversification journey of IEX. By 
extending its market expertise beyond electricity and natural gas 
into environmental products, ICX is creating new opportunities 
for market-based climate solutions while supporting India’s 
broader clean energy ambitions. As renewable energy 
capacity continues to expand and sustainability commitments 
become increasingly central to corporate strategy, ICX is well 
positioned to deepen the adoption of I-REC(E), broaden market 
participation and strengthen India’s clean energy market 
ecosystem. Through this initiative, ICX is enabling businesses 
to seamlessly align with global sustainability frameworks while 
contributing to the country’s long-term energy transition.
INDIAN COAL EXCHANGE: BUILDING THE 
MARKET ARCHITECTURE FOR INDIA’S COAL 
ECONOMY
Earlier in 2026, IEX incorporated Indian Coal Exchange to 
support the next phase of India’s Coal Economy.
For decades, India’s coal sector is focused on increasing 
domestic production to meet the country’s growing energy 
demand. Today, the challenge is evolving to ensure that coal 
production is discovered, priced, traded and allocated more 
efficiently. India produced a little over 1.0 billion tonnes of coal 
in FY’26 and production is expected to reach 1.5 billion tonnes 
by FY’30 and 1.8 billion tonnes by FY’35. While coal’s share in 
power generation is projected to decline from 71% in FY’26 to 
50% by FY’35, absolute share of coal in Indian energy mix shall 
continue to grow. This is supported by the fact that, production from captive and commercial mines crossed 200 million tonnes 
for the first time in FY’26 and is projected to reach 500 million 
tonnes by FY’35.  
This marks a structural shift in India’s coal market. As 
supply expands and market participants increase, efficiency, 
transparency and price discovery are becoming as important as 
production itself. Recognising this transition, IEX incorporated 
the Indian Coal Exchange Limited, extending its expertise in 
building transparent and efficient marketplaces to India’s coal 
sector.
CREATING A MARKET FOR A MUL TI-SELLER 
COAL ECONOMY
Policy reforms over the past few years have transformed the 
structure of the coal market. Commercial coal mining has 
removed the end use restrictions encouraging wider private 
participation. While captive mines were permitted to sell up to 
50% of their production in the open market. Consequently, Coal 
India’s share of domestic production has declined from around 
80% in FY’22 to 74% in FY’26, while captive and commercial 
mines now contribute 20% and SCCL accounts for 6%. 
Although Coal India sold around 11% of its production through 
e-auctions in FY’26, a significant share of surplus coal from 
captive and commercial mines continues to be traded through 
bilateral arrangements. As tradable volumes increase, a multi-
seller market requires transparent price discovery, standardised 
contracts and efficient mechanisms for matching buyers and 
sellers.
LAYING THE FOUNDATION FOR EFFICIENT 
COAL MARKETS
The notification of the Coal Exchange Rules, 2026, following 
amendments to the Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, has established the regulatory framework for 
exchange-based coal trading.
The Indian Coal Exchange has the potential to create 
transparent domestic benchmark prices, improve procurement 
efficiency and strengthen market visibility across the coal value 
chain. Beyond facilitating transactions, it can support better 
allocation of domestic coal, improve market competitiveness 
and contribute to more efficient utilisation of the country’s 
growing coal resources.
The incorporation of the Indian Coal Exchange reflects IEX’s 
commitment to building the market infrastructure needed for 
India’s evolving energy landscape. As the coal sector becomes 
larger, more competitive and increasingly market-driven, IEX 
is poised to support the next phase of India’s coal economy 
through greater transparency, efficiency and robust price 
discovery.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsDear Shareholders,
India remains a source of stability and opportunity amidst 
geopolitical tensions, inflationary pressures, and changing 
supply chains. In FY’26, India sustained its position as one 
of the world’s fastest-growing major economies, delivering a 
GDP growth of 7.7%, supported by the strength of domestic 
consumption, expanding capital investment, and steady 
industrial and services momentum.
India’s ascent in the global economic order, once a projection, 
has become an unfolding reality. Sustained economic growth, 
a bold national vision of building a Viksit Bharat by 2047, and a 
series of transformative reforms, including GST rationalisation, 
new labour laws, and landmark free trade agreements with the 
UK and the EU, are together reshaping the country’s economic 
landscape.
Looking ahead to FY’27, the RBI projects GDP growth to average 
6.6%, a resilient trajectory even as global headwinds persist. 
The country’s sustained investment and capital expenditure 
cycles, driven by both public infrastructure spending and 
rising private sector confidence, continue to lay the foundation 
for a $5 trillion economy well before 2030. India’s growth is 
reshaping the global economic landscape.
POWER SECTOR: STRENGTHENING FROM WITHIN
India’s power sector in FY’26 entered an important new phase, 
one where efficiency, flexibility, and access became as important 
as demand growth itself. At 1,708 billion units, overall electricity 
consumption remained largely stable year-on-year, influenced 
by an extended monsoon season and milder summers. Even 
so, the sector made measurable and meaningful progress in 
capacity creation, supply conditions, and market participation, 
providing a clear signal that the system is strengthening 
structurally.
The year witnessed a record incremental capacity addition 
of 58 GW across thermal and renewable sources, taking 
India’s total installed capacity to 533 GW. Of this, renewable 
energy now accounts for over 50% at 275 GW, making India 
the world’s third largest in renewable capacity. In fact, India 
achieved this milestone five years ahead of its 2030 target 
under the Paris Agreement. As the share of renewables grows, 
power exchanges become an increasingly important channel 
in ensuring electricity reaches consumers efficiently and at 
competitive prices.
Fuel availability in FY’26 further bolstered market stability. 
Domestic coal production crossed one billion tonnes, while coal 
inventories remained at a comfortable 25 days. This favourable fuel supply environment enhanced supply side liquidity on the 
exchange platform, leading to a competitive price discovery.
The average DAM price in FY’26 stood at `3.86/unit, lower 
by 14% compared with FY’25. This translated into a power 
procurement advantage for DISCOMs and C&I consumers.
POLICY AND REGULATORY LANDSCAPE: BUILDING DEEPER 
POWER MARKETS
FY’26 was a year of substantial policy action that is reshaping 
India’s power markets for the long term. Several landmark 
developments merit attention:
1. The Ministry of Power released the Draft National Electricity 
Policy 2026, charting India’s power sector roadmap aligned 
with Viksit Bharat goals, targeting per capita electricity 
consumption of 2,000 units by 2030 and over 4,000 units by 
2047. Additionally,
• The draft policy prioritises cost-reflective tariff reforms, 
a phased reduction in cross-subsidies, and time-of-day/
peak-hour pricing to improve efficiency and strengthen 
DISCOM finances.
• As per the draft, in order to promote competition, State 
Commissions may allow multiple licensees in the same 
area.

=== page 32 ===
• 
28 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statements• The draft policy emphasizes the role of Resource 
Adequacy at the State and Central level to better 
manage distributed energy resources (DER) and ensure 
grid stability.
• For deepening power markets, suitable policy and 
regulatory framework shall be established for generation 
capacity addition through market mechanisms such 
as bilateral contract settlements.  Further, the draft 
proposes the following for power markets:
a) Electricity from long term PPAs may be encouraged 
to be routed through power exchanges or any other 
platform recognized by the Central Commission. 
b) Central Commission will explore introduction of 
capacity markets in a phased manner to ensure 
required capacity addition.
c) A market-based system for consumer participation 
via demand response individually or through 
aggregators.
d) Regulatory frameworks to enable aggregation of 
DRE, small storage systems, and demand response 
mechanisms to increase market participation. India 
Energy Stack shall be established as a foundational 
framework for interoperable energy systems and 
seamless financial settlements.
e) The Appropriate Commissions shall facilitate long-
term Open Access for consumers by ensuring stable 
and predictable Open Access charges, along with 
unidirectional and progressively reducing trajectory 
of cross-subsidy and additional surcharges. 
f) Hedging of price and volume risks by market 
participants and progressively introducing forward 
contracts
g) In addition to market-based procurement, SCED 
and SCUC may be expanded to optimize power 
procurement costs; may be extended to other 
generators beyond ISGS.
h) As the markets mature and liquidity increases, 
interventions in power market operations will be 
discouraged. Any intervention should be based 
on established regulatory mechanisms, for a 
limited period and may be extended only after 
comprehensive analysis and consultation with 
stakeholders by the Central Commission.
2. Proposed amendments to the Draft Electricity (Amendment) 
Bill, 2025 are expected to strengthen DISCOM finances, 
progressively eliminate cross-subsidies for manufacturing 
and metro sectors, and significantly expand open access for C&I consumers, suggesting a transformative shift for 
exchange-based market participation.
3. The CERC issued final Virtual Power Purchase Agreement 
(VPPA) guidelines in December 2025, formally recognising 
power exchanges as authorised platforms for VPPA-based 
electricity sale by RE generators. This new market model 
is expected to meaningfully expand exchange volumes 
as corporate sustainability mandates accelerate VPPA 
adoption.
4. The Ministry of Environment issued final Greenhouse Gas 
Emission Intensity (GEI) targets for seven sectors, covering 
approximately 16% of India’s total GHG emissions. With 
carbon credit certificate trading procedures being drafted 
by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, the regulatory foundation 
for trading Carbon Credit Certificates on power exchanges 
is now being laid.
5. MNRE approved a 500 MW pilot Contract-for-Difference 
(CfD) for RE on a 3-hour basis to be implemented by SECI, 
a landmark step enabling RE generators to sell electricity 
through power exchanges, with SECI settling the price 
difference backed by a CfD Stabilisation Fund. This mirrors 
global models that have accelerated renewable capacity 
addition in the UK and Germany, and paves the way for 
merchant capacity addition in India.
6. Amendments to the REC Regulations 2026, the finalisation 
of Renewable Consumption Obligations (RCOs), and 
CERC’s approval of IEX’s green contract modifications have 
brought greater clarity to renewable energy procurement, 
supporting higher renewable participation on the exchange.
7. In FY’26, Ministry of Power introduced the India Energy 
Stack, a digital public infrastructure (DPI) aimed at digital 
protocols to ensure interoperability among utilities, 
regulators, and consumers, functioning similar to the 
UPI. Among the most applicable use cases of such an 
infrastructure would be the facilitation of P2P trading. 
India Energy Stack will enable seamless integration of 
currently uncaptured generation capacity into the market, 
significantly expanding tradable volumes on exchanges 
and driving a sharp rise in Open Access consumers
On market coupling, CERC issued draft regulations in April 
2026 proposing Grid India as the Market Coupling Operator. We 
continue to engage actively with the regulator, and through the 
legal process where warranted, to ensure that any structural 
change strengthens, rather than dilutes, the price discovery 
and efficiency that competitive markets have delivered for 
participants. Through this period of regulatory developments, 
we continue to invest in deeper customer relationships, a 
more resilient technology platform, and greater value for every 
participant on our exchange.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsIEX BUSINESS PERFORMANCE: A YEAR OF ROBUST GROWTH
IEX delivered a strong performance in FY’26, with annual 
electricity trade reaching 141 billion units, underscoring a 
17% growth over the previous year. This growth is especially 
significant given that the first half was shaped by softer demand 
conditions, demonstrating the underlying structural strength of 
exchange-based power trading.
The Real-Time Market (RTM) emerged as the defining growth 
story of FY’26. RTM volumes grew 41% year-on-year to 55 
billion units, now accounting for nearly 40% of total electricity 
volumes on IEX. This growth underscores the growing 
importance of flexibility in power procurement. As renewable 
energy becomes a larger share of India’s generation mix, the 
ability to respond in real-time to supply and demand variations 
becomes indispensable. 
The Green Market continued its steady progress, with traded 
volumes rising 23% over the previous year to 10.8 billion 
units. Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) trading remained 
active, with 187 lakh RECs traded, a 5% year-on-year increase, 
supporting compliance needs across obligated sectors. As 
RECs and green contracts become central to India’s energy 
transition, IEX’s role as the primary market infrastructure for 
renewable compliance deepens further.
On the products front, we continue to engage with CERC on 
approval to extend the Term-Ahead Market (TAM) contract 
duration from 3 months to 11 months, the Green RTM proposal, 
and a petition seeking introduction of peak-DAM and peak-RTM 
segments to enable trading during high-demand morning and 
evening hours, introducing products that will deepen market 
liquidity and better serve our participants.
Financially, FY’26 was another year of consistent value creation. 
IEX’s consolidated revenue grew 13.6% to `747.0 Crore, and 
Profit After Tax increased 14.9% to `492.9 Crore. The Board of 
Directors announced a final dividend of `2 per share, equivalent 
to 200% of the face value, taking the total dividend for the 
year, inclusive of the interim dividend ( `1.5 per share), to `3.5 
per share, reflecting our continued commitment to rewarding 
shareholders.

DIVERSIFICATION: BUILDING INDIA’S MUL TI-MARKET ENERGY 
GROUP
IEX’s vision extends well beyond electricity. Our diversification 
agenda is systematically transforming IEX into India’s leading 
multi-market energy group, spanning gas, carbon, and now 
coal.
The Indian Gas Exchange (IGX) completed five years of 
operations in FY’26 and continues to strengthen its position 
as India’s premier gas exchange. Representing close to 3% of 
India’s total gas consumption and 20% of the spot market, IGX 
traded 76.8 million MMBtu in FY’26, a 28% year-on-year growth, 
driven by demand from domestic producers, the power sector, 
and city gas distribution companies. IGX achieved a Profit 
After Tax of `41.9 Crore, 35% higher than the previous year, 
reflecting both operational scale and growing market adoption. 
Indian Energy Exchange holds 47.28% stake in IGX, and as per 
PNGRB regulations, it has to bring it holding down to 25%. IGX 
has initiated its IPO process. The Offer comprises an offer for 
sale of up to 22.28% equity shares by IEX, and remains subject 
to receipt of applicable approvals, market conditions, and other 
relevant considerations. The IPO aims to unlock further value 
for the gas market and for IEX shareholders.
Our wholly owned subsidiary, ICX, is gaining significant traction 
as India’s only accredited International Renewable Energy 
Certificate (I-REC) issuer. In FY’26, ICX issued 179 lakh I-RECs, 
highlighting a growth of over 200% compared with the previous 
year, with revenue rising to `7.7 Crore. As India’s voluntary 
carbon and clean energy markets mature, ICX is positioned 
to play an expanding role in helping organisations meet their 
global sustainability commitments.
We are now also taking forward India’s first Coal Exchange. 
Following the Ministry of Coal’s Final Regulations for a Coal 
Exchange, our Board has accorded in-principle approval to 
explore this opportunity, and we have registered a wholly 
owned subsidiary, Indian Coal Exchange Limited, for the same. 
With the Final Rules requiring existing e-auction platforms 
to transition to Coal Exchange trading within six months of 
operationalization, the opportunity size in the very first year 
itself could be about 100 million tonnes. Additionally, we are 
exploring the opportunity to set up a Minerals Exchange as

THE ROAD AHEAD: A FUTURE OF OPPORTUNITY
The long-term outlook for India’s power sector is compelling. 
With electricity demand projected by CEA to approach 2,700 
billion units and peak demand of 388 GW by FY’32 and GDP 
growing at 7–8% per annum, the coming decade will demand 
significant investment in generation, transmission, storage, and 
market infrastructure. Power exchanges will be at the center 
of this transition. Over the next few years, several structural 
growth opportunities will shape our journey:
1. Electrification of the Economy — Rising industrialisation, the 
expansion of railways and metro networks, and the broad-
based shift from fossil fuels to electricity across sectors 
are structurally increasing India’s electricity intensity. As 
the economy electrifies, power demand will grow well 
beyond historical patterns, creating sustained headroom 
for exchange-based procurement by DISCOMs, industries, 
and open-access consumers.
=== page 35 ===
• 
/ 
Annual Report 2025-26 | 31
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statements2. Data Centres and the AI Economy — India is witnessing 
a rapid surge in data centre capacity, driven by the digital 
economy, cloud adoption, and the AI revolution. Data 
centres are large, round-the-clock electricity consumers 
with strong incentives to procure renewable power to meet 
sustainability mandates. As hyper-scalers and co-location 
operators scale up in India, their demand for green power 
through market mechanisms will grow substantially.
3. Electric Vehicles and Charging Infrastructure — India’s EV 
transition is gaining momentum, and with it comes a new, 
distributed source of electricity demand. As EV penetration 
rises across personal, commercial, and public transport 
segments, charging infrastructure will require grid-scale 
power, with much of it optimally procured through market 
platforms. Exchanges can play a key role in enabling cost-
effective, time-of-day optimised power procurement for 
charging operators, and in integrating vehicle-to-grid 
capabilities as the ecosystem matures.
4. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — Large-scale 
BESS additions, with over 43 GWh supported through VGF 
mechanism and rapid decline of discovered tariffs, will 
play a transformative role in the market. BESS will absorb 
surplus solar generation during the day and deliver power 
during peak evening and morning hours, directly boosting 
exchange-cleared volumes. FY’26 marked the first 
merchant BESS trades on IEX, from Juniper Green Energy, 
followed by ACME Solar and Adani Green, bringing a new 
class of market participants and validating the storage 
arbitrage model.
5. New Market Mechanisms — The emergence of VPPAs, 
Contract-for-Difference, electricity derivatives, and Firm and 
Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) tenders will deepen 
market liquidity and broaden participation. The structural 
over-sizing inherent in FDRE projects will generate surplus 
generation that flows to exchanges, boosting both buy and 
sell liquidity. Electricity derivatives, now live on MCX and 
NSE, are expected to deepen spot market participation by 
enabling participants to hedge price risk.
6. Green Markets : Growing renewable generation and 
competitive green power prices have fueled participation 
in the Green Market. The Green Market segment has 
consequently recorded a three-year CAGR of over 50% and 
now accounts for nearly 8% of the electricity traded on the Exchange. Going forward, innovative products such as the 
Green Real-Time Market (Green RTM) will play a critical 
role in managing renewable variability and enabling greater 
renewable energy integration. Complementing these market 
developments, the REC market, also presents a growing 
opportunity for both compliance and voluntary procurement
7. Carbon  Markets — The Carbon Credit Certificate market, 
expected to commence trading by FY’27, represents a 
significant new revenue stream for IEX. With emission 
intensity reduction targets now notified for seven industrial 
sectors and compliance timelines approaching, obligated 
entities will need a transparent, market-based platform 
for carbon credit trading, a role IEX is uniquely positioned 
to fulfil through its exchange infrastructure and regulatory 
standing. 
8. Innovative RE Tendering and P2P Markets — The shift from 
plain-vanilla solar and wind tenders to firm and dispatchable 
models such as FDRE and RTC is creating new sell-side 
liquidity on exchanges. In parallel, the rise of rooftop solar, 
with installed capacity now reached 30 GW, and the push by 
states such as Karnataka, Delhi, and Uttar Pradesh towards 
peer-to-peer trading frameworks signal the emergence of a 
local energy market ecosystem where exchanges will play a 
central enabling role.
At IEX, we remain steadfastly focused on customer centricity, 
technology excellence, product innovation, and governance 
integrity, which have been the foundation of our leadership 
as India’s leading energy exchange for the past 18 years. We 
will continue to invest in our customers, our platform, and 
our people; expand our presence across energy markets; and 
play an enabling role in India’s energy transition. IEX’s strong 
governance structure and business fundamentals will continue 
to deliver value for all our stakeholders and for the nation.
I thank each one of you, our shareholders, customers, regulators, 
partners, and the dedicated IEX team, for your continued trust 
and support. Together, we are building an energy market that 
powers India forward.

40 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsINDIAN ECONOMIC REVIEW
The Indian economy maintained its strong growth momentum 
for the most part in FY’26 despite the global economy passing 
through a phase of significant transition and uncertainty. In this 
global environment, India continued to stand out as one of the 
fastest-growing major economies in the world growing steadily 
by 7.7% in FY’26. India’s impressive growth has been supported 
by robust private consumption, sustained government capital 
expenditure, a resilient financial sector, and the continued 
beneficial effect of income-tax and GST rationalisation 
introduced in the Union Budget 2025-26.
The country is steadily moving towards becoming a global 
economic powerhouse and continues to be on track to become 
a 5 trillion-dollar economy by FY’30. While global economic 
uncertainty is expected to remain elevated in FY’27 the RBI 
expects India’s GDP growth to average 6.6 per cent based on 
heightened risks of inflationary pressures, supply disruptions 
and slower global growth. On the domestic front, the Indian 
Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast a below-
normal South-West monsoon for 2026 at approximately 92% 
of the Long-Period Average (LPA), partly influenced by the 
development of El Niño conditions. This presents a headwind 
for the agricultural sector and rural consumption for FY’27.

INDIA’S POWER SECTOR
Countrywide electricity demand in FY’26 was 1,707 BUs, a 
marginal year-on-year increase of approximately 1%, reflecting 
a moderation in the pace of demand growth over FY’25. 
The slowdown was primarily driven by an early onset of the 
Southwest monsoon in May 2025, which reduced cooling needs 
and agricultural pump usage, compressing cooling-degree 
days significantly. Nevertheless, India’s long-run power demand 
drivers of rising income levels, rapid urbanisation, government 
electrification initiatives, expanding manufacturing, and electric 
vehicle adoption remain firmly intact. 
The power sector continued its rapid structural transformation 
in FY’26 with record-breaking capacity addition. India’s total 
installed generation capacity reached 533 GW as on 31st 
March 2026, an addition of 58 GW in a single year, the highest-
ever annual increment. India’s renewable installed capacity (excluding large hydro) crossed 230 GW, driven by record 
solar additions. A total of 55 GW of non-fossil capacity was 
added, the highest ever in a single year. Solar capacity surged 
to approximately 150 GW, while wind capacity rose to 57 GW. 
Total non-fossil capacity as on 31st March 2026 stood at 283 
GW (including large hydro and nuclear).Renewables (including 
large hydro) now account for approximately 53% of total 
installed capacity, a milestone. During this fiscal, India achieved 
50% non-fossil installed capacity nearly five years ahead of its 
2030 target. 
Renewable power generation during FY’26 increased 
significantly as solar generation grew 24% year-on-year, and 
wind generation rose 28% over the same period. Coal-fired 
generation however, declined by approximately 3.2%, the first 
contraction in several years, reflecting the growing contribution 
of clean energy to the grid. Total power generation in FY’26 
reached 1,848 BUs compared with 1,842 BUs in FY’25. 
This fiscal also witnessed growing grid integration challenges 
including curtailment of power, underscoring the urgent need 
to expand transmission and storage infrastructure alongside 
renewable capacity. The intermittent nature of renewable 
sources continues to necessitate innovative storage solutions. 
Both the Government and the private sector are actively 
exploring pumped storage, battery energy storage systems 
(BESS), and green hydrogen as means to ensure grid stability 
and drive India’s energy transition. In parallel, India has been 
pursuing clean energy goals through flagship initiatives 
including the National Solar Mission, the Green Energy Corridor 
Project , and the National Green Hydrogen Mission. All these 
initiatives are aimed at India’s committment to curtail the 
emissions intensity of its GDP by 45% by 2030 (relative to 
2005 levels) to restrict global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. 
India aims to establish a Green Hydrogen production capacity 
of at least 5 million metric tonnes annually by 2030 and the 
government has already commissioned nearly 8,000 tonnes 
per annum of production capacity across facilities. The Nuclear 
Energy Mission, announced in FY’26, adds nuclear power as a 
key pillar of India’s long-term energy security strategy, targeting 
100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047 through the newly enacted 
SHANTI Act, 2025. The PM Surya Ghar Yojana  continued to 
accelerate rooftop solar adoption, with more than 3.3 million 
rooftop systems installed as of May 2026, adding over 12 GW 
of rooftop solar capacity.
ELECTRICITY VALUE CHAIN
The electricity value chain starts with electricity generation, 
using sources such as fossil fuels, renewables or nuclear 
energy. Generated power is then transmitted via high-voltage 
networks over long distances to substations and distributed 
to homes, businesses and industries through low-voltage 
=== page 45 ===
\  
I • 
Annual Report 2025-26 | 41
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial Statementsnetworks. These components work together to ensure reliable 
and efficient energy delivery.
In India, rising power demand driven by population growth, 
evolving lifestyles and changing consumption patterns 
requires continuous investment in generation, transmission 
and distribution to ensure reliable and quality power supply. 
To cater to this consumption growth, under its ‘Power for All’ 
initiative, the Government of India aims to deliver reliable 24x7 
electricity supply at competitive rates to all consumers. 
GENERATION 
With energy shortages at the national level having reduced, 
reflecting the grid’s growing reliability, India in the post-Covid 
era has managed peak power demand consistently in excess of 
240 GW. In FY’26, peak demand touched 245 GW, slightly lower 
than the record 250 GW on an all-time basis reached in FY’25, 
According to the CEA, India’s total power generation in FY’26 
reached 1,848 BUs, with 71% generated from thermal, 10% 
from hydro, 16% from renewables (excluding large hydro), and 
3% from nuclear, respectively. Renewable energy’s share in total 
generation rose to 29.2% in FY’26, up from approximately 17% 
in FY’25 on an aggregate basis, highlighting the accelerating 
energy transition. In terms of capacity, total installed capacity 
in this fiscal stood at 533 GW with an incremental capacity of 
58 GW which was majorly accounted for by 55 GW of non-
fossil capacity addition. The share of non-fossil sources in 
total installed capacity now stands at 53% while coal-based 
capacity addition saw a structural decline to a share of 43%. 
The incremental capacity addition in the renewable space was 
led by additional solar capacity of 45 GW, wind capacity of 6.1 
GW, large hydro capacity of 3.4 GW and nearly 1 GW of nuclear 
capacity.

TRANSMISSION
The nation’s regional grids remain seamlessly interconnected 
under the ‘One Nation One Grid One Frequency’ framework. The 
inter-regional capacity has increased by more than 75% since 
2014, reflecting sustained investment in grid infrastructure. 
This integrated system enables efficient electricity distribution 
across all regions, strengthening the reliability and resilience 
of the entire power network. As of March 31st, 2026, India’s 
interregional transmission capacity of the National Grid stood at 
over 120 GW, with transmission line length and transformation 
capacity continuing to expand significantly. India’s national 
transmission network has crossed a major milestone 
exceeding 5 lakh circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission lines 
and reaching a total transformation capacity of 1,407 gigavolt 
amperes (GVA). By reinforcing both generation and networks 
simultaneously, India has laid the foundation for a power sector 
that can support growth not just today, but well into the future. 
The National Electricity Plan (2023–2032) for Central and State 
transmission systems has also been finalised to meet the  
projected peak demand by 2032 and involves an estimated 
investment of over `9 lakh crore.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsDISTRIBUTION
In FY’23, the Ministry of Power introduced the Electricity (Late 
Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules to bolster 
the financial viability of the power sector. These rules were 
subsequently amended in FY’24 to address un-requisitioned 
surplus power. In FY’25, the National Load Dispatch Centre 
(NLDC) revised the procedure to include State-owned 
generating stations, with mock runs for penalties on generators 
commencing from July 2025. In FY’26, these rules became 
fully operational, further enhancing generator compliance, 
improving payment discipline and power market liquidity. 
Over the past few years, the government has introduced key 
measures to strengthen power distribution:
• Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS):  The 
implementation of RDSS has continued to incentivise 
utilities under the `3 lakh crore scheme, targeting reduction 
of pan-India AT&C losses to 12–15% and the ACS-ARR 
gap to zero. The progress has been steady, with smart 
meter deployment reaching 22% of approved installations 
as of December 2025. Time-of-Day (ToD) tariffs were 
mandated for all non-agricultural users from April 2025, 
aligning consumption patterns with solar generation.
• Additional Borrowing Scheme: State Governments 
continue to access additional borrowings of up to 0.5% 
of GSDP , conditioned on undertaking and sustaining 
power sector reforms to ensure financial viability of their 
Discoms.
• Prudential Lending Norms: Additional norms targeting 
financially stressed utilities remain in force. Discoms 
failing to meet defined improvement trajectories remain 
ineligible for borrowings from PFC and REC.
• Automatic Fuel Cost Pass Through: Several States have 
continued to employ automatic fuel and power purchase 
cost adjustment mechanisms, ensuring financial 
sustainability of Discoms.• Integrated Discom Ratings: Earlier in March, the 14th 
Annual Integrated Rating and Ranking Report for 65 
Discoms was released, evaluating their financial health, 
performance excellence and responsiveness to external 
factors. According to the report, 41 utilities were able to 
achieve reduction in AT&C losses. A total of 22 utilities 
recorded an improvement in their ratings, while 30 utilities 
maintained their existing ratings. AT&C losses reduced for 
39 utilities in FY’25, with 38 utilities achieving AT&C losses 
below 15%, reflecting enhanced operational efficiency. 
According to the report, at the national level, AT&C losses 
have declined from nearly 16.0% in FY’24 to 15.0% in 
FY’25.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsECONOMIC EXPANSION AND POWER MARKETS
Industrial Growth and Urbanisation
Industrial growth and urbanisation remain key elements in 
India’s economic development and ongoing power sector 
transformation. The Government’s thrust on Atmanirbhar Bharat  
and policy measures to position India as the cornerstone of 
the China Plus One strategy for global businesses augmented 
exports and domestic productive capacities in FY’26. This was 
despite global trade uncertainties. These policy measures 
continue to drive increased electricity demand from the 
manufacturing sectors.
India has achieved notable strides in urbanisation. It is 
projected that by 2030, over 40% of India’s population will be 
living in cities. Although these cities occupy only about 3% 
of the country’s total land area, they remarkably generate 
60% of India’s GDP . India’s rapid urbanisation is projected to 
significantly increase energy consumption. Further, expected 
electricity demand from the growth of AI and data centres is 
also factored into the planning process of the government as it 
reinforces long-term demand projections. This AI growth boom 
is driven by cloud adoption, data localization mandates, and 
localized Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) workloads. As per 
the Ministry of Power, electricity demand from data centres is 
estimated to touch nearly 14 GW by FY’32. The strong growth 
in data centre demand is likely to trigger parallel demand for up 
to 50 GW of renewable energy. In the near term power demand 
is expected to touch almost 2,700 BUs with a peak demand of 
388 GW by FY’32.
Demand and Supply
According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), all India 
energy consumption reached approximately 1,707 Billion Units 
(BU) in FY’26, representing a year-on-year growth of about 1.1% 
from 1,692 BU in FY’25. The moderation in demand growth 
was primarily driven by an early onset of the monsoon in May 
2025, which reduced cooling degree days by more than 7% 
compared to 2024, with a 12% decline in June alone, a month 
which typically accounts for about 15% of annual demand. The 
peak demand met during the summer in FY’26 was 242 GW 
recorded in June 2025, while in June FY’25 peak demand stood 
at 245 GW.
The Northern Region remained the largest contributor to 
demand, though due to weather related events growth rates 
varied significantly across regions in FY’26. Key States such 
as Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Uttar 
Pradesh recorded the highest peak demand levels.Energy Met Comparison of Top States — FY’25 vs FY’26

Short-Term Electricity Market
According to the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(CERC), India’s short-term power market volumes stood at 
approximately 302 BU in FY’26 compared with 238 BU in FY’25. 
Short term transactions accounted for 13% of total generation 
of 1,848 BU. The short-term market itself has grown at a CAGR 
of 8.9% from FY’10 to FY’25.
Within the short-term market, power exchanges remained the 
dominant segment, facilitating 60% of short-term transactions, 
while bilateral transactions, including trades through energy 
traders and direct agreements between distribution companies 
contributed 26% to the market share. The Deviation Settlement 
Mechanism (DSM) accounted for 13%. This steady expansion 
of the short-term electricity market underscores the growing 
reliance on dynamic and competitive electricity procurement 
methods to meet rising energy demands and enhance market 
efficiency.
OUTLOOK
In FY’26, India demonstrated remarkable resilience in navigating 
a complex global environment characterised by geopolitical 
tensions, evolving trade policies, and climate-linked demand 
volatility. India’s strong macroeconomic fundamentals, robust 
private consumption, fiscal consolidation, and sustained public 
capex continue to underpin healthy power demand growth over 
the medium term. With India firmly on its trajectory to remain 
the world’s fastest-growing major economy, the power market 
is well-positioned to capitalise on annual incremental demand 
of nearly 100 BUs projected through 2030. The accelerating 
shift towards renewables, rising need for market-based storage 
dispatch supported by the government’s push on addition of 
BESS and PSP , introduction of newer market mechanisms, 
the structural load shifts in agriculture, and expansion of open 
access participation provide sustained growth levers for power 
market development.

44 | Indian Energy Exchange Limited
Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsELECTRICITY SEGMENT
In FY’26, IEX achieved its highest-ever electricity traded volume 
of 141 BU, a 17% year-on-year increase over nearly 121 BUs 
traded in FY’25. This performance was driven by strong growth 
in the Real-Time Market and the Green Market, even as national 
power demand growth moderated. Several factors contributed 
to this increase:
• Weather Variability: The  arrival  of  early  and  prolonged  
monsoons  moderated  power  demand.  The Indian 
Metrological Department reported 8% higher rainfall 
during this fiscal’s monsoon, the highest rainfall in five 
years, which helped support higher hydro generation.
• Record Renewable Generation:  Solar generation rose 
24% on a year-on-year basis and wind generation rose 
28% YoY in FY’26, providing abundant supply, particularly 
during solar hours.
• Higher Supply Liquidity: Enhanced wind, hydro, and 
solar generation alongside sustained coal-based supply 
resulted in sell-side liquidity which was higher by nearly 
50% on a year-on-year basis on the exchange platform, 
and consequently deepend market participation.
• Decline in Electricity Prices: The Market Clearing Price 
in the Day-Ahead Market fell to `3.86/unit in FY’26, lower 
by 14% YoY from `4.47/unit in FY’25, while the Real-Time 
Market price declined to `3.59/unit to be lower by 16% YoY 
from `4.28/unit. These prices encouraged greater market 
participation.
• Optimisation by DISCOMs and Open Access (OA) 
Consumers:  DISCOMs and OA consumers continued 
to strategically optimise power procurement, taking 
advantage of competitive exchange prices.
Day-Ahead Market
In FY’26, a total of 62.8 billion Units (BU) were traded in the Day-
Ahead Market (DAM, including HP-DAM), an increase of 2.4% 
over FY’25. DAM accounted for approximately 44% of total 
electricity volumes on IEX. The average daily volume traded in 
DAM was approximately 172 MU.
Real-Time Market
The Real-Time Market (RTM) was the standout performer 
in FY’26, trading 54.9 BUs, a 41% year-on-year increase and 
accounting for approximately 39% of total electricity volumes traded on IEX. The daily average volume in this segment was 
approximately 150 MU. This segment was also witness to a 
strong last quarter with volumes of 14.3 BU, a rise of 48.2% 
year-on-year, reflecting the growing preference for flexible, 
real-time electricity procurement.
Term-Ahead Market
The Day-Ahead Contingency and Term-Ahead Market (TAM), 
comprising HP-TAM, contingency, daily, weekly, and monthly 
contracts up to 3 months, traded 12.7 BUs in FY’26, an increase 
of 8.0% year-on-year. TAM accounted for approximately 9% 
of total electricity volumes. The Longer Duration Contract 
(LDC) continues to serve as a flexible alternative to traditional 
procurement platforms, offering buyers the ability to procure 
power for up to 90 days. IEX has also filed a petition with the 
Hon’ble CERC seeking extension of delivery duration of the 
contracts from 90 days to 11 months and continues to await 
regulatory approval.
Green Market
The Green Market, comprising the Green Day-Ahead Market 
(G-DAM) and the Green Term-Ahead Market (G-TAM), achieved 
10.8 BUs of volumes in FY’26, an increase of 23% on a year-
on-year basis. The average price in G-DAM for FY’26 was 
`4.36/unit, a decline of 10.6% compared with FY’25, reflecting 
improved renewable supply liquidity. The share of Green Market 
volumes accounted for nearly 8% of total electricity traded on 
IEX.

Corporate Overview Statutory Report Financial StatementsCERTIFICATE SEGMENT
Renewable Energy Certificate (REC)
The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) REC 
Regulations 2022, which went into effect from December 
5th, 2022 and were fully implemented in FY’24, continued to 
govern the REC market. The regulations permit RECs to be 
perpetually valid (till sold), with no floor or forbearance price, 
and introduced technology multipliers (Wind & Solar – 1; Hydro 
– 1.5; Municipal Waste – 2; Biomass & Biofuel – 2.5). RECs 
are traded on exchanges twice a month, providing consumers 
competitive rates.
CERC has directed GRID-India to review trends in REC 
transactions and propose measures for further increasing 
auction frequency beyond the current twice-a-month schedule, 
with stakeholder consultations ongoing. REC fungibility and 
elimination of the floor price have enhanced market liquidity, 
with REC inventory levels close to 3.9 crore certificates at the 
close of FY’26.Trading volumes of RECs remained strong in FY’26 with a total 
of 187.20 lakh (18.72 million) RECs traded, representing nearly 
18.72 BUs of electricity, higher by 5% on a year-on-year basis. 
As with other segments on the exchange, the last quarter ended 
very strong and saw 71.71 lakh RECs being traded. This marked 
the highest-ever annual REC trading volume on IEX, reflecting 
the growing significance of RECs in promoting renewable 
energy adoption and ensuring efficient market participation.
Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts)
The Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) mechanism, a market-
based tool introduced by the Indian Government, aims to 
enhance energy efficiency in energy-intensive industries. 
Designated Consumers (DCs) assigned targets are rewarded 
with Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) for surpassing them 
or required to purchase certificates if they fall short. 
In FY’26, ESCerts were at a major juncture as India prepares to 
transition the high greenhouse gas-intensive sectors from the 
Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme into the new Carbon 
Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS).
